extracted.intended_audience: students, poets, dramatists, and literary critics studying classical rhetoric and poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes classical criteria (Aristotle, Demetrius, Longinus) for composing and evaluating poetry, drama, and elevated prose—covering plot, character, style, rhetorical proofs, and the sources of the Sublime. Useful for creative writers and literary students applying ancient standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (mythos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the most important component of tragedy; the arrangement of incidents (action) should be the chief object of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot should present a complete action with a beginning, middle, and end; priority over character—events drive the work. Avoid loose episodic sequences; aim for causal necessity and probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should represent one complete and unified action rather than a series of disconnected events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate irrelevant subplots or digressions; each scene should contribute to the single coherent line of action and lead toward resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude/Wholeness (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work must have appropriate magnitude and a structurally whole form: a clear beginning, middle, and end to achieve completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure appropriate length and scale for full development of the action; balance complexity with intelligibility so the whole can be apprehended as one whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex Plot: Peripeteia and Anagnorisis
rubrics_metrics.description: The most effective plots include reversal of fortune (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnorisis), often combined, producing profound emotional effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-timed reversals and discoveries to create surprise and necessity; they should arise naturally from the plot, not be artificially contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia / Tragic Error (cause of suffering)
rubrics_metrics.description: A protagonist’s error or frailty (hamartia) that precipitates catastrophe—often a mistake in judgment or action—is central to tragic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The error should be plausible and linked to the character’s situation, not gratuitous wickedness. It should elicit pity and fear rather than simple blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eliciting Pity and Fear; Catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy’s purpose is to arouse pity and fear and effect catharsis (purging or purification) of these emotions in the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange incidents and character fate to move the audience ethically and emotionally toward a cathartic resolution. Avoid sensationalism that manipulates emotions without moral or intellectual consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: Consistency, Propriety, and Likelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be believable and consistent, acting in ways appropriate to their nature and role in the plot; they should reflect types rather than implausible extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters need not be morally perfect; their actions must be intelligible within the story’s moral world and necessary for plot development. Avoid sudden, inexplicable changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) — Ideas and Reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should express sound thought: the arguments, themes, and reasoning that arise in speech and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use speeches and incidents to reveal character and theme. Thought is measured by the quality of ideas, argument, and the persuasive power of what is said.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (lexis) — Appropriate Language and Metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Language and choice of words are essential: appropriate diction, apt metaphors, and clarity of expression contribute to artistic success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select words suited to character, genre, and occasion; employ metaphor for insight, not ornament alone. Avoid obscure or affected phrasing that obscures meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song/Melody (melos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical elements (chorus, lyric) are a constituent of tragedy and should be integrated harmoniously into the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lyrical and musical moments to enhance emotional effect and unity; they should be subordinate to plot and not disrupt narrative coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (opsis) — Visual Effect as Lesser but Potent
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual elements (staging, spectacle) are powerful but less artistic than plot and character; spectacle can amplify but not replace intrinsic poetic excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ visual show to support, not substitute for, poetic craftsmanship. Beware reliance on spectacle to hide weaknesses in plot or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical Proofs: Ethos, Pathos, Logos
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasion relies on three forms of proof: character (ethos), emotion (pathos), and argument (logos). Effective rhetoric balances them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop speaker credibility, stir appropriate emotion, and construct sound logical argument. Overreliance on any one mode weakens overall persuasive force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five Canons of Rhetoric: Invention, Arrangement, Style, Memory, Delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical production involves inventing material, arranging it persuasively, choosing suitable style, committing it to memory, and delivering it effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to each stage: find persuasive arguments and examples, order them for maximum effect, match language and ornament to purpose, and prepare delivery to suit audience and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement/Disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Order and structure of parts (introduction, narration, proof, refutation, peroration) should follow logical persuasive progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange material to build toward an effective climax; transitions should be smooth and each section serve the rhetorical aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness/Decorum (to prepon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style and subject-matter must be appropriate to one another and to the audience: tone, diction, and ornament should suit the theme and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match register and figures to genre and audience expectations; grand language is misplaced in trivial subjects, and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, Purity, and Correctness of Language (Demetrius)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language should be clear, pure, and correct; obscurity and error undermine style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simplicity and correctness over artificial complexity; correct grammar and idiom are essential to persuasive and beautiful style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament and Figures of Speech (balanced use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures (metaphor, simile, antithesis, etc.) enrich style but must be used with judgment so ornament serves meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ rhetorical figures to illuminate thought and affect the hearer/reader. Avoid excessive or irrelevant ornament that distracts from substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness vs. Affectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Expression should feel natural and inevitable rather than forced or merely rhetorical; authenticity strengthens impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate spontaneity and conviction in phrasing; contrived effect and mannerism diminish authority and reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of the Sublime (Longinus) — Greatness of Thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Sublimity begins with lofty and noble thought: grandeur of conception and idealizing vision elevate language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for elevated ideas that reveal greatness of soul or profound insight; trivial or petty subject-matter cannot be made sublime by language alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of the Sublime — Strong Emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Intense, genuine emotion energizes language and produces sublime effects when it informs diction and rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let passion breathe through expression so energy and urgency shape syntax and image. Avoid manufactured sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of the Sublime — Figures and Vivid Imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold, apt figures and striking metaphors contribute to sublimity by making abstract greatness sensorial and memorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favour original, powerful metaphors and comparisons; clichéd or worn-out images deflate potential sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of the Sublime — Noble Diction and Elevated Phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of words, cadence, and elevated phraseology contribute materially to the sublime effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dignified, sonorous language and varied rhythm; avoid mean or pedestrian words in passages meant to be lofty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of the Sublime — Dignified Composition and Amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangement, rhythm, and amplification—gradual buildup and climax—produce transport in the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure passages to ascend in intensity and revelation; craft cadences and sentence-length variation to carry the reader upward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and Force (avoid imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine sublimity and excellence arise from original force of mind and feeling, not from mere imitation of lofty models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek personal intellectual and emotional resources; do not rely on imitating formulas or borrowed phrases that lack inward conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on the Reader (transport, elevation, awe)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate test is the audience’s response—sublime and excellent works transport, move, and elevate the reader or hearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success by the work’s ability to produce intense, coherent, and morally or intellectually significant emotional responses rather than by technical display alone.
